system: You answer questions about two pictures of physical systems. Use the tool answer once per question; an answer cannot be changed and you are not told whether it is right. When you cannot tell, give your best estimate and say so in your message. When every question is answered, end with a short message that says which answers you read from a picture and which you inferred. The two pictures, A and B, are attached to the task, in order.
task:
Two pictures are described below.
Picture A: three trajectories of balls launched from the ground at one speed and three angles, and a wall.
Picture B: the displacement against time of a mass on a spring, released from rest at two amplitudes.

Answer every question with the tool answer.
1. (picture A) Can this launcher, at its speed and at any angle from 10 to 80 degrees, land a ball more than 45 m away? Answer with the option's number: 1 yes; 2 no.
2. (picture A) Which of the three drawn trajectories passes over the wall? Answer with the option's number: 1 the 20-degree trajectory; 2 the 45-degree trajectory; 3 the 70-degree trajectory; 4 none of them.
3. (picture A) If gravity were half as strong and the launch the same, the landing distance of the 45-degree trajectory would be: Answer with the option's number: 1 halved; 2 unchanged; 3 doubled; 4 four times larger.
4. (picture A) Read the landing distance of the 20-degree trajectory. Answer in m, between 0 and 60.
5. (picture B) Read the period of the oscillation. Answer in s, between 0 and 3.
6. (picture B) If the mass were released from twice the larger amplitude, its period would be: Answer with the option's number: 1 halved; 2 unchanged; 3 doubled; 4 four times larger.
7. (picture B) An instrument reads the displacement at any time from 0 to 3 s, with the same noise at every time, and you want the frequency. When does one reading tell you most about it? Answer with the option's number: 1 in the first second; 2 in the last second; 3 equally at every time.
8. (picture A) At the top of the 45-degree trajectory, which way does the ball accelerate? Answer with the option's number: 1 up; 2 down; 3 zero; 4 forward, along the motion.
9. (picture B) When the displacement passes through zero, the speed of the mass is: Answer with the option's number: 1 zero; 2 the largest it reaches; 3 half the largest it reaches.

steps.text: I opened both pictures. Picture A: launch speed 20 m/s. The 20-degree and 70-degree trajectories both land at about 26 m, the 45-degree one lands at about 40.5 m, and the wall stands at about x = 30 m and is 5 m high. Picture B: both amplitudes have the same period, about 1.5 s. Here are my answers to questions 1 to 4.
Questions 1 to 4 are recorded. Here are my answers to questions 5 to 8.
Questions 5 to 8 are recorded. Here is my answer to question 9.

All nine questions are answered. Read directly from the pictures: Q2 (45 degrees passes the wall; the 20- and 70-degree balls land at about 26 m, short of the wall at about 30 m, and the 45-degree ball is still about 8 m high there, above the 5 m wall), Q4 (about 26 m, read from the axis to within about 1 m, and it matches 400 sin40 / 9.81 = 26.2 m), and Q5 (1.5 s, the time between the peaks at 0, 1.5 and 3.0 s). Read from the picture and checked by calculation: Q1 (no; the farthest landing is the 45-degree one at about 40.5 m, and the largest possible range v^2/g = 400/9.81 = 40.8 m is under 45 m) and Q6 (unchanged; the picture shows the same period at both amplitudes, as expected for a linear spring). Inferred from physics rather than read: Q3 (the range is v^2 sin(2 theta)/g, so halving g doubles it), Q7 (the last second; the change in displacement for a small change in frequency grows with time, as A t sin(omega t), so later readings say more about the frequency, assuming the amplitude is known), Q8 (down; gravity is the only acceleration), and Q9 (the largest speed; at the equilibrium point all the energy is kinetic). Q7 is the answer I am least sure of, because it depends on that assumption.
